176.title: Vayera: visiting the sick (Genesis 18:1)
176.hook: God appears to Abraham as he heals; the rabbis learn that God visits the sick (Sotah 14a)
176.tomorrow: Vayera: shall not the judge do justly?
176.howItsDone: Visiting the sick is a mitzvah in Jewish law; some synagogues have bikur cholim volunteers who visit hospitals and homes, and the Mi Sheberach prayer for healing is said during the Torah reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, new names: Abram became Abraham, Sarai became Sarah, and the covenant of circumcision began. Your line was a name can grow. Today, a new portion: Vayera.

When someone's sick, it can be hard to know what to do. What do you say? Will a visit intrude? Maybe they want rest. So a text goes out instead: a heart emoji, get well soon. The fourth portion of the Torah opens with a single quiet verse: God appears to Abraham, sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day. It doesn't say why. But the rabbis looked at where this verse sits, right after Abraham's circumcision, and drew a conclusion that became a whole Jewish practice.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SAY?` → `A TEXT, A HEART EMOJI.` → `GOD APPEARS AT THE TENT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Vayera, and he appeared, from its first verse: "And the LORD appeared unto him by the terebinths of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." Why does God appear? No message, no command. Just presence. The rabbis noticed that the verse right before tells of Abraham's circumcision, at ninety-nine. So Abraham is recovering, sore, sitting in the shade. The Talmud says God came to visit the sick, to ask after his welfare. Then it builds a whole teaching on it. The Torah says to walk after the LORD your God. How can a person walk after God? By copying God's ways. God clothed the naked, Adam and Eve; so you clothe the naked. God visited the sick, Abraham; so you visit the sick. God comforted mourners, Isaac after his father died; so you comfort mourners. God buried the dead, Moses; so you bury the dead. The Hebrew for visiting the sick is bikur cholim: bikur, a visit, and cholim, the sick. It's a mitzvah, a commandment, and some Jewish communities have a bikur cholim group whose whole job is to show up. The Talmud even says a visitor takes away a small part of the illness, one sixtieth. It's not medicine. It's company. The rabbis give the visitor practical advice too: don't sit up high over the sick person; sit at their level. And they expect a visitor to ask for mercy for the one who is sick. Just by showing up, the rabbis say, a visitor does what God did at a tent door on a hot day.

segments.voice: Think of someone who's sick, hurting or recovering, near or far, and picture yourself sitting beside them, at their level, not standing over them. You don't need to say anything clever; just be there. If you pray, ask for their healing; if you don't, hold them in mind with warmth.
Bikur cholim. Visiting the sick: a Jewish commandment learned from God, who appeared to Abraham as he healed.

177.title: Vayera: shall not the judge do justly? (Genesis 18:25)
177.hook: Abraham asks "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?"
177.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often point to Abraham's plea for Sodom as the model for arguing with God on behalf of justice, a thread that runs through the prophets, the Psalms and Hasidic stories.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bikur cholim: God appeared to Abraham as he healed, and visiting the sick became a way of walking after God. Your line was visit the sick.

Pushing back on someone with far more power is its own hard skill. A boss. A judge. A doctor. A parent, years ago. Every word gets chosen carefully: with respect, I don't think that's fair. In this portion, someone says that to God. Three visitors have eaten at Abraham's tent and are heading toward Sodom, and God decides to tell Abraham what's about to happen to that city. What Abraham says next is a question about God's own justice.
screen: `PUSHING BACK ON POWER.` → `THE VISITORS HEAD TOWARD SODOM.` → `ABRAHAM PUSHES BACK ON GOD.`

segments.voice: First, the text lets you hear God weighing it: shall I hide from Abraham what I am doing? God decides not to, because Abraham is meant to teach his children to do righteousness and justice. So God says: the outcry from Sodom is great, and its sin is very grievous. And Abraham steps forward. Would you destroy the righteous with the wicked? What if there are fifty righteous people in the city? That be far from you. And then the line: "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" Think about who he's saying it to. God agrees: for fifty, I'll spare the whole place. Then Abraham keeps going. I, "who am but dust and ashes," what if there are forty-five? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Ten? Each time, God says yes. Abraham stops at ten, and the story leaves it there. Notice three things. First, Abraham is arguing for strangers. Sodom isn't his city; its king is the one whose wealth he refused. He argues for them anyway. Second, he's humble and bold at once: dust and ashes, and still asking. Third, God doesn't rebuke him. Some readers go further: God shared the plan because Abraham is meant to teach justice, so speaking up is the point. Later Jewish voices pick up the thread: Moses pleading for his people, Jeremiah and Job asking why, and in Hasidic stories, a rebbe who calls God to a trial on behalf of his people. In this story, the man chosen to teach justice is the one who asks God for it.

178.title: Vayera: Abimelech (Genesis 20)
178.hook: a foreign king turns out more upright than Abraham feared
178.howItsDone: Jewish commentators read Genesis 20 as a story in which Abraham's fear of strangers proves mistaken, and note that here God calls Abraham a prophet who will pray for the king.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vayera, Abraham argued for a city of strangers: shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly? Your line was justice, even from God.

You move to a new town, or start a new job, or travel somewhere far away. Before you've met anyone, you've already decided a few things. People here are cold. People here can't be trusted. Better keep your guard up. Sometimes that instinct protects you. And sometimes it's just wrong, and the people you braced against turn out to be decent. Abraham, the great hero of this portion, the one who just argued for strangers, walks into a foreign town with exactly that fear.
screen: `BEFORE YOU'VE MET ANYONE.` → `KEEP YOUR GUARD UP.` → `ABRAHAM WALKS INTO GERAR.`

segments.voice: Abraham and Sarah travel to Gerar, ruled by a king named Abimelech. Abraham tells people Sarah is his sister, not his wife. So Abimelech, thinking she's unmarried, takes her into his house. That night God comes to Abimelech in a dream and warns him: she's a married woman. Abimelech, who hasn't touched her, protests. He asks God, in effect, will you destroy even a righteous nation? He said she was his sister. She said he was her brother. I did this with a clean heart and clean hands. Listen to that question. It echoes Abraham's own from yesterday, shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly, now in the mouth of a foreign king. And God agrees: I know you did this with a clean heart; that's why I kept you from sinning. Return her. The text adds something: Abraham is a prophet, and he'll pray for you. In the morning Abimelech calls Abraham and asks: what did you see, that you did this thing? And Abraham answers: "Surely the fear of God is not in this place." He assumed these people had no conscience. The story shows otherwise. Abimelech returns Sarah, gives sheep and oxen and servants, and says: my land is before you; live wherever you like. Then Abraham prays for Abimelech's household, and they're healed. The story lets the founder of the Jewish people be wrong about strangers, and lets a foreign king be the one with the clean heart.

179.title: Vayera: Isaac is born (Genesis 21:1–7)
179.hook: God remembers Sarah, and she says all who hear will laugh with her
179.howItsDone: Genesis 21 is read in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, when, tradition says, Sarah was remembered; the birth of Isaac is often taught alongside Sarah's two laughs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a foreign king in Gerar turned out more upright than Abraham feared. Your line was goodness is everywhere. Today, a promise twenty-five years long comes true.

There are two kinds of laughter. One is the short, dry laugh when someone tells you something impossible. Oh, sure. Right. That'll never happen. The other bursts out of you when the impossible thing happens anyway. The baby is born. The test comes back clear. The person you gave up on walks through the door. Almost the same sound, from a completely different place. Sarah laughs both ways in this portion. Today, the second laugh.
screen: `OH, SURE. RIGHT.` → `THE IMPOSSIBLE HAPPENS ANYWAY.` → `SARAH LAUGHS BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: A few chapters back, three visitors came to Abraham's tent, and one said: this time next year, Sarah will have a son. Sarah, about ninety, was listening from inside the tent. She laughed to herself: after I'm worn out, and my husband is old, shall I have pleasure? God asked Abraham: why did Sarah laugh? "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" Sarah, afraid, said, I didn't laugh. The answer came back: no, you did laugh. That was the first laugh. Now, chapter twenty-one. God remembered Sarah, as promised, and did for her as God had spoken. In her old age, at exactly the time foretold, she gives birth to a son. Abraham names him Yitzchak, Isaac, which means he will laugh. And Sarah says: God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh with me. Then, almost in wonder: who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? The same laugh, turned inside out, from disbelief to joy. And she doesn't keep it to herself. Rashi, following the midrash, says that when Sarah was remembered, many other childless women were remembered with her, many sick people were healed, many prayers were answered, and there was laughter in the whole world. This chapter is read in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah; the tradition says Sarah was remembered on that day. So every Jewish year begins with a laugh that turned from doubt to joy.

segments.voice: Think of a time something you'd given up on actually happened, big or small, and remember the laugh or the smile that came out of you. Let it come back into your face now, even a little. Then picture the people you'd want to share it with, and let the joy spread out to them: everyone who hears will laugh with me.

180.title: Vayera: here am I (Genesis 22:1, 7, 11)
180.hook: Abraham answers "here am I" to God, to his son and to the angel
180.tomorrow: Chayei Sarah: the life of Sarah
180.howItsDone: The binding of Isaac, the Akedah, is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and some Jews recite it in the daily morning prayers; hineni is also the name of a prayer the cantor says before the additional (Musaf) service on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in some communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaac was born, and Sarah's laugh turned from doubt to joy. Your line was laugh with me. Today, the last day of Vayera, and its hardest chapter.

Someone calls your name from the next room. Yeah? What? In a minute. Half your mind is still on what you were doing. Now think of the few times you answered with all of you. A child crying at night, and you're up before you're awake. A friend on the phone, and you hear that something's wrong, so you put everything down. Hebrew has a word for answering like that. It's not just yes. It means: I'm here, fully. Abraham says it three times in one chapter.
screen: `YEAH? WHAT? IN A MINUTE.` → `ANSWERING WITH ALL OF YOU.` → `ONE WORD, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: The word is hineni. Here I am. The chapter is Genesis twenty-two, which Jews call the Akedah, the binding of Isaac. Jewish readers have argued over it for a long time. It begins: "God did prove Abraham, and said unto him: 'Abraham'; and he said: 'Here am I.'" God tells him to take his son, his only son, whom he loves, Isaac, and offer him up on a mountain. Abraham rises early and goes. On the third day, father and son walk up the mountain together, Isaac carrying the wood. Isaac speaks: "My father." And Abraham says: "Here am I, my son." The same word. Isaac asks where the lamb is, and Abraham says God will provide. At the top, when Abraham has bound Isaac and taken up the knife, an angel calls from heaven: Abraham, Abraham. A third time he answers: here am I. Don't lay your hand on the boy, the angel says. Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it instead. Isaac is not harmed. Readers disagree deeply about this story. Some see Abraham's complete faith. Some read it as a rejection of child sacrifice. Some modern readers ask why the man who argued for Sodom says nothing here. Whatever they make of it, they keep coming back to the word. Hineni, to God. Hineni, to his son. Hineni, to the angel who stops him. Fully present to each. Later, when God calls, the prophet Isaiah will answer: "Here am I; send me." So that's Vayera: a visit to the sick, an argument for justice, a stranger's goodness, a laugh of joy, and here am I.

181.title: Chayei Sarah: the life of Sarah
181.hook: a portion called "the life of Sarah" begins with her death
181.howItsDone: Chayei Sarah is read in synagogues each autumn, and many Jews remember loved ones by telling stories of their lives at shivah, the week of mourning, and on each yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hineni: Abraham answering here I am, to God, to his son, to the angel. Your line was here I am.

Sarah dies in the first two verses of a Torah portion named for her life. It's called Chayei Sarah, the life of Sarah. It tells how long she lived, then that she died, then that Abraham came to mourn her. Every year, Jews read a portion named for her life that opens with her death. Readers have made something of that. Today: why the name is life.
screen: `NAMED FOR HER LIFE.` → `CHAYEI SARAH: THE LIFE OF SARAH.` → `IT OPENS WITH HER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Portions take their names from words near their start, and here the first words are these, in the Jewish Publication Society's old translation: "And the life of Sarah was a hundred and seven and twenty years; these were the years of the life of Sarah." It doesn't say Sarah died at a hundred and twenty-seven. It says her life was that long, and then it says so again. The Hebrew counts strangely, too: a hundred years, and twenty years, and seven years, each with its own word for years. Rashi, the medieval commentator, read that slowly. Each stage is counted on its own, he said, because each was whole. At a hundred she was as free of wrongdoing as she had been at twenty, and at twenty as lovely as at seven. And the closing phrase, these were the years of the life of Sarah: Rashi says all of them were equally good. Not only the famous ones. The waiting years, the laughing year, the old years. There's a harder side, too. The portion comes right after Abraham takes Isaac up the mountain, and an old midrash connects the two: Sarah died, it says, when she heard what had happened to her son. The text itself is silent about that. What it does say is that Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her. So the portion holds both: a real death, real grief, and a name that points past it. Readers take the name as a lesson: when you remember someone, you choose which word goes on the door. Here, the word is life.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even a pet, and skip past the ending for a moment. Find one ordinary scene from their life: a kitchen, a car ride, something they always said. Stay in that scene, and let them be alive in it for a while.
Chayei Sarah. The life of Sarah: a Torah portion that opens with her death, and is named for her life. Chayim, life, is the same word in the toast l'chaim.
Your line: the portion is called life. Her years come first, then her death. That's day one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: Chayei Sarah: to mourn and to weep (Genesis 23:2)
182.hook: before the cave and the silver, Abraham mourns; what to do when a friend is sitting shiva
182.howItsDone: After a funeral, the closest relatives traditionally sit shiva at home for seven days, pausing for Shabbat; friends and neighbors visit, bring meals, often join prayers so mourners can say Kaddish, and let the mourners lead the conversation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chayei Sarah: a portion named for her life. Your line was the portion is called life. Today, the verse between her death and everything that follows.

A message comes in: my dad passed away. We're sitting shiva at the house this week. And you freeze. Do I go? Do I bring something? What do I say? Is it a party or a funeral? On day forty-nine, Abraham bought a cave to bury Sarah. But the verse just before the buying is about something else. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." Grief first, then the paperwork. Today: how Jewish tradition shows up for a mourner.
screen: `"WE'RE SITTING SHIVA."` → `DO I GO? WHAT DO I SAY?` → `GRIEF FIRST.`

segments.voice: Shiva means seven. After a funeral, the closest family stays home for seven days, and the community comes to them. The Torah has an early echo: when Jacob dies, Joseph "made a mourning for his father seven days." Comforting mourners has its own name, nichum avelim, and the rabbis counted it among the kindest things a person can do. So, the practical part. Yes, go, if the family has shared the times. Often the door is left unlocked so nobody has to keep getting up; you can walk in quietly. Mourners may sit on low stools, and mirrors may be covered. Bring food, not flowers: feeding the mourners is the old custom, and in many families flowers aren't. Then the hardest part, what to say. The tradition's answer is surprising: very little at first. The Talmud teaches that comforters shouldn't speak until the mourner speaks. Job's friends got this right for seven days, sitting with him on the ground in silence, and only went wrong when they started explaining. So sit down and let them lead. If they want to talk, ask about the person. A story, a memory, their laugh: that's the gift. Skip everything happens for a reason. As you leave, many say a traditional line, may God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. If you don't know it, I'm so sorry and a hug are plenty. And if the grief you're carrying is your own and it feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS AT HOME.` · `WALK IN QUIETLY; BRING FOOD.` · `LET THE MOURNER SPEAK FIRST.` · `ASK ABOUT THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Picture a living room with the chairs pushed together, a table of food, a family sitting low, and yourself coming in quietly and sitting down, without a speech ready. Notice the urge to fill the silence, and let it pass. If someone you know is grieving now, hold them in mind; if the grief is yours, picture someone sitting with you, saying nothing, just staying.
Nichum avelim. Comforting mourners: going to them, feeding them, and letting them speak first.
Your line: show up, say less. Being there is what a shiva visit is for. Day one hundred eighty-two, done.
